extracted.intended_audience: students and practitioners of literary criticism, essayists, and writers interested in style, metaphysics, and religious writing
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for writing and judging literary, philosophical, and religious prose—emphasizing clarity, choice of words, temperament in criticism, and how to render abstract thought intelligible to readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Render metaphysics sensible
rubrics_metrics.description: "The true science of metaphysics consists not in rendering abstract that which is sensible, but in rendering sensible that which is abstract; apparent that which is hidden; imaginable, if so it may be, that which is only intelligible; and intelligible, finally, that which an ordinary attention fails to seize.",
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Metaphysical writing should make abstract ideas tangible and apparent. The aim is to make what is obscure graspable by ordinary attention rather than to veil the sensible in abstraction. Treat metaphysics as communicable to non‑specialists.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distrust words not in common currency
rubrics_metrics.description: "Distrust, in books on metaphysics, words which have not been able to get currency in the world, and are only calculated to form a special language.",
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid inventing or relying on arcane technical vocabulary that has not become part of ordinary usage; such words form a special jargon that distances readers and signals imperfect metaphysics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use words in their popular or natural sense rather than a special philosophical sense
rubrics_metrics.description: "Which is the best, if one wants to be useful and to be really understood, to get one's words in the world, or to get them in the schools... to employ words in their popular sense rather than in their philosophical sense; and the better plan still, to employ them in their natural sense rather than in their popular sense.",
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Definitions and terminology should reflect the common, 'natural' acceptation when possible. Defining a term purely philosophically 'binds him who makes them' and proves little unless the definition matches the world‑wide sense. Novel or private definitions are acceptable in scholastic fencing but not when seeking public understanding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid proving matters of sentiment by dry argument
rubrics_metrics.description: "Do not bring into the domain of reasoning that which belongs to our innermost feeling. State truths of sentiment, and do not try to prove them.",
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For matters of faith, feeling, and deep moral sentiment, avoid converting them into problems for logical proof—argumentation can make what is accepted by feeling appear doubtful. Instead present such truths in a way that fosters belief (make people believe, do not prove them).

rubrics_metrics.name: Make truth lovely rather than arm it
rubrics_metrics.description: "Make truth lovely, and do not try to arm her; mankind will then be far less inclined to contend with her.",
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Presentation (beauty, clarity, charm) matters for persuasion: attractive expression invites acceptance, while over-defensive, combative argument provokes attack. In religious and literary exposition, aim to show truth's beauty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Employ familiar/common words to seize the reader
rubrics_metrics.description: "It is by means of familiar words that style takes hold of the reader and gets possession of him... these words make a style frank and easy... what one says in such words looks more true; for, of all the words in use, none are so clear as those which we call common words; and clearness is... one of the characteristics of truth.",
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer common, well‑worn words to ornate or artificially coined expressions to create trust, clarity, and an easy, convincing style. Common words help ideas gain currency and appear truthful.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be profound with clear terms; keep charm when going deep
rubrics_metrics.description: "Be profound with clear terms and not with obscure terms. What is difficult will at last become easy; but as one goes deep into things, one must still keep a charm... carry into these dark depths of thought... the pure and antique clearness of centuries less learned than ours, but with more light in them.",
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When treating deep or difficult subjects, maintain lucid expression and an appealing style; complexity of thought should not be disguised by obscure language—clarity enhances depth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid personifying technical terms and talismanic phrasing
rubrics_metrics.description: "The trick of personifying words is a fatal source of mischief in theology." (example: 'The Jansenists erect "grace" into a kind of fourth person of the Trinity.')
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not allow technical or emotive words to be treated as autonomous agents or talismans; instead translate them into clearer, more concrete terms (e.g., 'grace' → 'help, succour, a divine influence') to break misleading spell‑like effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prioritize clear and consoling truths over obscure ones in exposition
rubrics_metrics.description: "We ought to lay stress upon what is clear in Scripture, and to pass quickly over what is obscure; to light up what in Scripture is troubled, by what is serene in it... The Jansenists have done just the reverse.",
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In interpreting scripture or other complex texts, emphasize the luminous, consoling, and accessible truths rather than dwelling on puzzling, dismal, or overly abstruse doctrines; bring obscure passages into relief via the clear ones.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid excess cross‑national literary arrogance ('saugrenu' judgments)
rubrics_metrics.description: The essay discusses that "the literary judgments of one nation about another are very apt to be saugrenus... a foreigner's judgments about the intrinsic merit of a nation's authors will generally... be wrong; but there is a permissible wrongness... When that limit is exceeded, the wrong judgment becomes... saugrenu, or impudently absurd.",
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be wary of sweeping condemnations or extravagant praise of another nation's literature; allowances exist for honest difference, but critics exceed propriety when they make impudently absurd cross‑cultural claims (examples: Coleridge's judgments on French literature).

rubrics_metrics.name: Criticism and scholarship must be informed—ignorance is a grave literary fault
rubrics_metrics.description: "Ignorance, which in matters of morals extenuates the crime, is itself, in matters of literature, a crime of the first order.",
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Writers and critics must be well‑informed; sloppy or ignorant literary judgments are a serious fault. Thorough knowledge is a prerequisite for fair criticism.

rubrics_metrics.name: To persuade in religion (or similar domains) one must possess the conviction one seeks to transmit
rubrics_metrics.description: "You may do what you like, mankind will believe no one but God; and he only can persuade mankind who believes that God has spoken to him. No one can give faith unless he has faith; the persuaded persuade, as the indolgent disarm.",
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authenticity and conviction in the speaker/writer are essential for genuine persuasion—those who truly believe are the effective persuaders; mere argument from the unconvinced is futile.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not substitute jargon, artificial ideas, or ciphers for native ideas and values
rubrics_metrics.description: "Not one [system of metaphysics] has succeeded; for the simple reason, that in every one ciphers have been constantly used instead of values, artificial ideas instead of native ideas, jargon instead of idiom.",
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Systems that rely on empty symbols, artificial constructs, or technical jargon rather than rooted, idiomatic ideas tend to fail. Preference should be given to natural idiom and native ideas in exposition and argument.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cultivate patience and the habit of refining ideas until they 'shine'
rubrics_metrics.description: Joubert praises "spirits, lovers of light, who, when they have an idea to put forth, brood long over it first, and wait patiently till it shines... genius to be the aptitude for patience..."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The writing process should include patient incubation and repeated refinement: allow ideas time to mature and be expressed in their clearest, most beautiful form rather than publishing prematurely.
